title: PXAPI shared acquisition definitions v1
description: Reusable lexical $defs the acquisition contracts reference. This file is not a contract: no document validates against it as a whole, and it carries no analysis meaning of its own. It exists rather than an extension of common.v1.json because common's $id pins it at 1.0.0 and every registered contract references that exact URI: adding a definition there would either leave the version lying about the file's content or break every existing reference. It holds the lexical URL and digest shapes of the acquisition slice, including the narrowings of those shapes: public_origin is referenced by site-inventory.v1 alone today and is declared here rather than in that carrier because it narrows the very authority segment public_url declares two lines above it, and one authority shape stated twice is the way the two drift apart. A vocabulary — a closed set of tokens with rules about what each token means — still belongs to the carrier that owns those rules, and none is declared here.

public_url.description: An absolute http or https URL that carries no userinfo component, as a structural shape only. It differs from common#/$defs/url in exactly one respect, and deliberately: the authority segment excludes '@', so a credential-bearing URL such as https://user:secret@example.com/ cannot become persisted canonical contract data. An empty userinfo ('https://@example.com/') is refused for the same reason. The '@' stays legal after the first '/', '?' or '#', because a path or query may contain one and nothing is being smuggled there. Everything else remains out of scope here: reachability, canonicalisation, redirect policy, egress rules, loopback and private ranges, and robots handling belong to the slice that owns the acquisition runtime, never to a contract. The authority and remainder are bounded separately and the group repeats at most once, so a hostile value cannot make matching super-linear.

public_origin.description: The lexical shape of a site origin: an absolute http or https URL that carries no userinfo, names an authority, and ends either there or at the normalised root slash. It is public_url narrowed, and the narrowing is the whole point — a member a reader treats as the authority for a whole site must not be able to hold one page of it, so a path beyond the root, a query and a fragment are each refused outright rather than tolerated and ignored. The authority's legal port form is permitted, because a site served on an explicit port is still a site, and the credential rule is inherited unchanged: '@' is excluded from the authority, so https://user:secret@example.com/ is refused here exactly as it is refused by public_url, and there is no remainder after the authority in which an '@' could become legal again. The bound follows from the shape rather than being chosen: the longest value this pattern admits is a scheme, an authority of 253 characters and the root slash. Everything beyond the lexical shape stays out of scope exactly as it does for public_url: reachability, DNS resolution, redirect policy, egress rules, loopback and private ranges, and robots handling belong to the slice that owns the acquisition runtime, and a value of this shape proves none of them.

url_key.description: The canonical identity of one discovered URL: the value under which observations that collapse to the same target are aggregated. It is a public_url, so an identity can never carry a credential. The rules by which two observed forms reduce to one key are the producer's canonicalisation method, which is named and versioned by the carrier rather than fixed here — this definition fixes the identity's lexical shape and nothing about how it was derived.

digest.description: A canonical content digest, written with its algorithm in the value: 'sha256:' followed by 64 lower-case hexadecimal characters. The algorithm is carried rather than implied, so a document never has to be read against an assumption about how its digest was produced, and a later algorithm is a new version of the carrying contract rather than an ambiguous hex string of a different length. Upper-case hexadecimal is refused so that one byte sequence has exactly one written digest. What the digest is computed over is stated by the member that carries it; this definition fixes only the shape.
